lead: A smart object is a small package of five blocks: it senses, computes, communicates, carries its own power and knows its identity. Pack those blocks into one node and the object can report on itself and act on a command. A sensor node, also called a mote, is the hardware core of this idea: it supplies sensing, computing, communication and power. Add actuation and identity and the node becomes a full smart object. You meet smart objects in home meters, factory vibration tags, smart parking sensors and crop-field nodes. The power budget, not the radio peak, decides how long a battery lasts.
prereq: You need: 2.1 and 2.2 for the sensing and actuation blocks.

sections.h3: Five blocks of a smart object

blocks.text: Five blocks make a smart object: processing, sensing and actuation, communication, power, and identification. The processing unit runs local logic. The sensing unit measures the world; the actuation unit changes it. The communication unit sends data and receives commands. The power unit supplies every block. The identification unit gives the object a name or address.

Three terms look alike. A sensor node (mote) is a small board with sensor, microcontroller, radio and battery; it usually senses and forwards data. A smart object adds actuation and identity, so it can act as well as report. An IoT device is the wider product, often one or more smart objects plus a network service. A sensor is not a smart object; it is one block inside it.

The awareness–representation–interaction view: the object is aware of its state, represents it in data, and interacts with users or other objects. That is a useful design lens, but the five blocks are the engineering content.

A sensor node has a sensing unit, a processing unit, a transceiver and a power unit. The sensing unit holds the sensor and an analog-to-digital converter (ADC). A 0–5 V signal into a 10-bit ADC gives 2¹⁰ = 1024 codes. The step is 5 V ÷ 1024 ≈ 4.9 mV, so smaller changes may not change the code.

The processing unit is a microcontroller with memory. It filters samples and decides when to wake the radio. The transceiver is often a 2.4 GHz low-power radio; it carries short packets. The power unit is a battery, a harvester or both. Some nodes add a location unit (GPS) or a mobility unit (motor, drone mount). The radio sets the peak current. The sleep current is set mainly by the microcontroller when it is not put into its deep-sleep mode, plus any leakage in the regulator and the sensor left powered.

sections.h3: Choosing the link and paying for it

blocks.text: Pick a link on nine criteria: range (distance), data rate (bits/s), duty cycle (fraction of time on), latency (delay), reliability (packets delivered), energy per useful bit (joules per delivered bit), topology (star, tree, mesh), cost (per node and gateway), and licence band (2.4 GHz is licence-free in most countries; cellular bands need an operator).

blocks.where: I<sub>avg</sub> is the average current in mA; D is the awake fraction (0 to 1); I<sub>awake</sub> and I<sub>sleep</sub> are the currents in mA during the awake and sleep states.

blocks.text: A node at 30 mA for 1 ms every 10 s has D = 0.0001 and adds only 3 µA to the average. A sleep leak of 50 µA costs more. Sleep current and duty cycle decide the battery, not the transmit peak. The worked example does the full sum.
The node program is a loop. Each pass does five jobs.

items: Sense: power the sensor and wait its warm-up time.
Convert: read the ADC and turn the code into a physical value.
Compute: filter, average or compare with a threshold.
Transmit: send only the result or a short packet.
Sleep: turn off sensor and radio, put the microcontroller into its lowest power mode, wake on a timer or interrupt.

blocks.text: Order matters. Sending every raw sample wastes energy and clogs the network. A mean of 100 samples sent once is often better. Sleep is a block, not an afterthought; forget it and the average current becomes the awake value. For actuation, add a command step before sleep: receive a setpoint, drive the actuator, then sleep.

examples.question: A sensor node runs on a 1000 mAh battery of which 80% is usable. It draws 8 mA for 200 ms every 60 s and 3 µA otherwise. Find the average current and the battery life in days and years.
steps: Awake fraction D = 200 ms / 60 s = 0.2 s / 60 s = 0.003333.
Sleep current = 3 µA = 0.003 mA. Sleep fraction = 1 − 0.003333 = 0.99667. Sleep average = 0.003 mA × 0.99667 = 0.00299 mA.
examples.answer: Average current 0.0297 mA; battery life 26 975 h ≈ 1124 days ≈ 3.1 years.
examples.check:
usable = 1000 * 0.8
D = 0.2 / 60
Iavg = 8 * D + 0.003 * (1 - D)
hours = usable / Iavg
days = hours / 24
years = days / 365
print(round(Iavg, 4))
print(int(round(hours)))
print(int(round(days)))
print(round(years, 1))

traps: A sensor is one block of a smart object, not a smart object. The object also needs processing, radio, power and identity.
Battery life follows average current. A high transmit peak for a short duty cycle may cost less than a constant sleep leak.
Convert µA to mA before adding: 3 µA = 0.003 mA, not 3 mA.
Duty cycle D is a fraction between 0 and 1. A 1% duty cycle is D = 0.01, not 1.
mAh is charge, mA is current. Divide usable mAh by average mA to get hours.

quiz.q: List the five blocks of a smart object.
quiz.a: Processing, sensing and actuation, communication, power, identification.

quiz.q: Give one line each for sensor node, smart object and IoT device.
quiz.a: Sensor node: small sense-compute-radio-power board. Smart object: adds actuation and identity so it can act. IoT device: wider product with one or more smart objects and a network service.

quiz.q: A node draws 10 mA for 100 ms every 10 s and 5 µA otherwise. Usable charge is 1000 mAh. Find average current and life in days.

Two nodes have the same 20 mA transmit peak. Node A sleeps at 1 µA and sends for 10 ms every minute. Node B sleeps at 100 µA and sends for 10 ms every 10 minutes. Which lasts longer? Show the average terms.
quiz.a: A: D = 0.01/60 = 0.000167; awake term 0.00333 mA; sleep term 0.001 × 0.999833 = 0.0009998 mA; total ≈ 0.00433 mA. B: D = 0.01/600 = 0.0000167; awake term 0.000333 mA; sleep term 0.1 × 0.999983 = 0.099998 mA; total ≈ 0.10033 mA. A lasts much longer; B's sleep leak dominates.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has a 0–3.3 V range. What is the step size?
Why does a sensor node need an identification unit?
quiz.a: So the sink, gateway or other nodes can address it and attribute readings or commands to the correct node.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, smart objects are moving to energy harvesting and intermittent computing, where a node may run only when a capacitor has enough charge. Matter and Thread push identity and commissioning into home devices. Research looks at tiny machine learning on microcontrollers so a node sends a label, not raw samples. Search for intermittent computing, backscatter sensor node, TinyML microcontroller and energy-neutral IoT to go further.
